notes: Cross-tier interop fixture for the signed-envelope wire protocol. Every Runar SDK (TS/Go/Rust/Python/Zig/Ruby/Java) must consume this and produce byte-identical canonical_json output + verify the valid envelope + reject each tampered envelope with the listed reason.

canonical_json_vectors._notes: Empty key MUST sort before astral plane char in UTF-16 code-unit order (not UTF-8 byte order). Gates Zig D1 fix.

Astral-plane char U+1F600 vs BMP char U+E000. UTF-16 sort: high surrogate 0xD83D < 0xE000 ⇒ astral first. UTF-8 byte sort: 0xF0… > 0xEE… ⇒ BMP first. Triggers a byte-vs-UTF-16 divergence that v18 misses (empty key compares equal under both orders).
Boolean false MUST be preserved verbatim. Gates Ruby D4 fix (the `value[k] || value[k.to_sym]` fallthrough silently rewrote falsy values).

Float at the ECMA-262 1e21 boundary MUST emit `1e+21`. The D5 divergence is fixed: every tier now emits the spec ECMA-262 Number::toString form via its `*Ecma262Double` formatter (Go appendEcma262Double, Rust format_ecma262_double, Python _format_double, Zig appendEcma262Double, Ruby format_ecma262_double, Java formatEcma262Double; TS uses the native JS formatter). `expected` is the spec form and is enforced as a byte-parity gate across all tiers.

Tiny float MUST emit `1e-300` (no trailing `.0`). The D5 divergence is fixed: every tier's `*Ecma262Double` formatter now emits the spec ECMA-262 Number::toString form, so all tiers produce `1e-300` (no trailing `.0`). `expected` is the spec form and is enforced as a byte-parity gate across all tiers.

canonical_json_rejection_vectors._notes: Lone surrogate (U+D800 with no low-surrogate partner) is invalid Unicode per RFC 8785 and MUST be rejected. The D6 fix has landed: every tier now rejects this input — TS (canonical-json.ts: lone-surrogate code path), Go (sdk_envelope.go: WTF-8 0xED,0xA0..0xBF detection), Python (envelope.py: 0xD800..0xDFFF check), Zig (sdk_envelope.zig: error.LoneSurrogate), Ruby (envelope.rb: U+D800..U+DFFF raise), Java (Envelope.java: Character.isHighSurrogate/isLowSurrogate check). Rust cannot represent a lone surrogate in its `&str` type at all (structurally rejected at the type boundary). The Go interop test `packages/runar-go/sdk_envelope_interop_test.go` (TestEnvelopeInterop_CanonicalJSONRejectionVectors) asserts this rejection against this vector. This vector now ENFORCES rejection across all tiers. The input is supplied as a UTF-16 code-unit array so each tier constructs the string deterministically without relying on its JSON parser's lone-surrogate handling.
canonical_json_rejection_vectors.description: object with a value containing the lone high surrogate U+D800

rejection_vectors._notes: The payload is well-formed JSON by the grammar but contains an UNPAIRED SURROGATE escape (\ud800 with no low-surrogate partner), so the string it denotes is not well-formed Unicode. Measured before the fix, on the same envelope: ts / go / python / java accepted it and fell through to 'bad-sig', while rust / ruby / zig rejected it at the parse step with 'bad-json' — four tiers against three, returning different VerifyEnvelopeReason for identical wire input. The project already holds that a lone surrogate is invalid Unicode and must be rejected (vector v22, audit D6); verifyEnvelope hashes the payload RAW, so canonicalJson's detector never sees it and each tier needs the check on the payload text itself.

01 is not a JSON number token at all (RFC 8259 forbids a leading zero), so the payload is bad-json, decided at parse time before the integer-token check. The signature is VALID for this exact payload text, so a tier whose parser accepts 01 as 1 returns ok:true instead of falling through to bad-sig. Inner nonce 01, outer 1. A raw U+0001 inside a string. RFC 8259 requires U+0000..U+001F to be escaped. Java's Json.readString appended it; the other six tiers rejected the payload.

\u+041 is not four hex digits. Java's Json.readString handed "+041" to Integer.parseInt(_, 16), which accepts a sign and returned 'A'.

allowlist_vectors_notes: GK-BUG-008. verifyEnvelope's optional pubkey allowlist. A caller that supplies NO allowlist (null) gets no allowlist check; a caller that supplies a list gets exactly that list, so an EMPTY list allows nobody. Before the fix Go read `len(ExpectedKeys) > 0`, so an empty (non-nil) slice skipped the check and returned ok:true where ts/rust/python/zig/ruby/java returned pubkey-not-allowed. Replay valid_envelope at verify_now_ms with the vector's expected_keys (null = the caller supplies no allowlist). The allowlist is the LAST check, after ECDSA, and valid_envelope's signature is valid, so a reason other than the one listed means the allowlist itself is wrong.

allowlist_vectors._notes: CONTROL. A fix that treated an absent allowlist like an empty one reddens here.
CONTROL. The signer's own key is listed.

clock_skew_vectors_notes: R-261. Every tier's verifyEnvelope takes an optional clock skew and an optional "now" override, and six of the seven distinguish an EXPLICIT ZERO from NOT SUPPLIED: TS `?? 5_000`, Rust `Option::unwrap_or`, Python default arg, Ruby kwarg (0 is truthy in Ruby), Zig struct default, Java's clockSkewMs field default. Go conflated the two -- `ClockSkewMs int64 // defaults to 5_000 when zero` -- so a caller asking for STRICT expiry silently got a five-second replay window. Measured on the valid envelope, 2000 ms past expiry with clockSkewMs explicitly 0: go ok:true, while rust/python/ruby/zig/java all said expired. The same zero-value-sentinel sat on Go's NowMs AND on Java's nowMs: with now explicitly 0 (the epoch, i.e. nothing can have expired yet) python and ruby returned ok:true while java returned expired, because 0 was read as "not supplied" and replaced with the wall clock. Both are now genuinely optional in both tiers. Each vector below names the OPTIONS a caller supplies: a null means the caller does NOT supply that option and the tier's own default applies -- that is the control with teeth, because a fix that made 0 strict by dropping the default would redden cs2. TS's verify reads Date.now() directly rather than taking an injectable clock, so it covers the skew half in its own unit tests against a live clock.

clock_skew_vectors._notes: 2000 ms past expiry, caller explicitly asks for zero tolerance. Expired on every tier. This is the row Go failed.

CONTROL. Same envelope, same clock, but the caller supplies NO skew, so the tier default of 5000 ms applies and 2000 ms of lateness is tolerated. An over-strict fix -- one that made explicit zero strict by removing the default -- reddens here.
CONTROL. 8000 ms past expiry with an explicit 10000 ms tolerance: accepted. Proves the caller's value is used rather than the default, in the direction the default alone would reject.

The now-override half of the same defect. now = 0 is the epoch, so an envelope expiring in 2023 has NOT expired yet. Go and Java read 0 as "not supplied" and substituted the wall clock, returning expired where python, ruby, rust and zig returned ok:true.

depth_vectors_notes: R-260. verifyEnvelope parses the payload with each tier's stock JSON library and used to inherit that library's recursion cap, which differs per tier. Measured on ONE envelope (priv=1, live clock, payload {"deep":<N-deep array>,...}): ts/go/python/zig accepted every depth probed (zig to 100001), ruby flipped to bad-json at total depth 101 (JSON.parse default max_nesting: 100), rust at total depth 128 (serde_json RECURSION_LIMIT), and JAVA THREW StackOverflowError OUT OF verify (Json.java readValue/readObject/readArray are mutually recursive with no cap and Envelope.verify catches Exception, not Error) -- at ~5000 deep on a default JVM stack and ~1000 deep under -Xss512k, i.e. the threshold was a JVM launch flag, not a protocol property. Every tier now enforces MAX_ENVELOPE_PAYLOAD_DEPTH = 100 (this file's payload_depth_limit) on the payload TEXT, with a NON-RECURSIVE bracket scan run immediately before the stock parser, so the answer is the same everywhere and the guard itself cannot overflow. depth = the number of containers enclosing a value, 1-based, outermost = 1; 100 accepted, 101 rejected. 100 is Ruby's native JSON.parse default EXACTLY and sits 27 below rust's 127, so no tier has to hand-roll or reconfigure its parser to stay inside it, and it is far above what the wire needs (deepest checked-in conformance artifact: depth 15; this file: 6). It is deliberately the SAME number as canonicalJson's emit-side bound -- if parse were the smaller of the two, a tier could emit a legal, correctly-signed envelope another tier is physically unable to parse. Over-limit rejects as bad-json, the reason two tiers already returned natively and the reason the R-115 lone-surrogate text guard uses.

depth_vectors._notes: Exactly at MAX_ENVELOPE_PAYLOAD_DEPTH (1 outer object + 99 nested arrays = 100). Validly signed by alice (priv=1). This is the control with teeth: an over-strict depth guard, or one that counts off by one, reddens HERE.

One level past the limit (1 outer object + 100 nested arrays = 101). Its signature is VALID for its payload, so a tier that fails to enforce the depth bound returns ok:true rather than a different rejection reason — the assertion cannot pass by accident on a bad-sig fallthrough.

duplicate_key_vectors_notes: R2-DUPKEY. verifyEnvelope REJECTS a payload in which any JSON object, at any nesting depth, has two members with the same key, compared after JSON string unescaping ("a", "\u0061" and a surrogate-pair spelling of the same code point are all one key). Reason bad-json, decided in the parse step: after too-large / missing-fields / expired, before envelope-mismatch / bad-sig / pubkey-not-allowed -- exactly where a malformed payload is decided. Before the fix TS/Go/Rust/Python/Ruby/Java kept one of the values (most the last) and verified ok; only Zig's std.json refused. Uniqueness is PER OBJECT: the dkc* controls are accepted. Replay each envelope at verify_now_ms. Every dk*/dkc* signature verifies for its exact payload text except dk11 (deliberately carries valid_envelope's signature to pin bad-json ahead of bad-sig). The OUTER envelope object is not covered here: no SDK tier parses an envelope from wire text -- verifyEnvelope takes an already-decoded structure.

duplicate_key_vectors._notes: Top-level key `kind` appears twice. JSON.parse / encoding/json / serde_json / json.loads / Ruby JSON.parse keep the LAST value, so before the fix this verified ok in those tiers while the signer and the verifier can disagree on what `kind` says.
Duplicate key in an object that is an array element; the two values are identical, which is still a duplicate.
"\u0061" and "a" are the same key after JSON string unescaping.
"a/b" and "a\/b" are the same key after unescaping.
A raw U+1F600 key and its escaped surrogate-pair spelling are the same key. Byte-oriented tiers must combine the pair before comparing.
Duplicate inner nonce; the LAST value equals the outer nonce. A keep-last parser saw a matching nonce and returned ok. Must be bad-json, never envelope-mismatch or ok.
Duplicate inner nonce; the FIRST value equals the outer nonce. A keep-first parser would return ok, a keep-last one envelope-mismatch. Must be bad-json.
"n\u006fnce" is `nonce`; both carry the outer value, so only duplicate detection after unescaping rejects it.
Duplicate key seven containers deep (well inside the R-260 depth bound).
PRECEDENCE: dk2's payload under valid_envelope's signature, which does not verify for this text. bad-json is decided at parse time, before ECDSA, so the reason is bad-json, not bad-sig.
PRECEDENCE: expired is decided before the payload is parsed, so an expired envelope with a duplicate key is expired, not bad-json. Outer nonce/expiresAt 1000000000000/1000000000001.
CONTROL: `a` appears in four DIFFERENT objects (top level, two array elements, m). Uniqueness is per object; a scanner with one global key set reddens here.
CONTROL: `a` in a parent and in its child objects is not a duplicate.
CONTROL: string VALUES that spell a key (including repeated array strings) are not keys.

malleability_vectors_notes: F-138 (CL-BUG-159 / CL-BUG-241). ECDSA signatures are malleable: if (r, s) verifies for a digest under a key, so does (r, N - s). BIP-62's low-S rule is a Bitcoin SCRIPT policy (SCRIPT_VERIFY_LOW_S) for transaction signatures; it is not part of the envelope protocol. The TS reference verifyEnvelope delegates to @bsv/sdk's raw ECDSA verify, which has no low-S check, so the reference ACCEPTS a high-S envelope signature. Measured on mv1 before the fix: ts / go / python / zig / java ok:true; ruby bad-sig (an explicit BIP-62 check in Runar::ECDSA.ecdsa_verify, now skipped for envelopes via low_s: false) and rust bad-sig (k256's verify_prehash rejects high-S outright; envelope.rs now normalizes s before verifying). Every signer in every tier still EMITS low-S; this section only pins what a VERIFIER must accept, which is the case an overlay backend meets when a client signs with a non-normalizing library or a relay malleates s. Every signature in the rest of this file is low-S, so without this vector the split was invisible. Replay each envelope at verify_now_ms with no allowlist; the vector's signature is valid for its payload, so a tier that rejects it can only do so on the low-S rule.

malleability_vectors._notes: valid_envelope with its signature's s replaced by N - s (DER re-encoded: s now has its top bit set, so it gains a 0x00 pad byte and the sig grows from 0x45 to 0x46 bytes). r, payload, pubkey, nonce and expiresAt are unchanged. Mathematically the same signature class as valid_envelope; the TS reference accepts it.

signing_vectors_notes: GAP-064 cross-tier signing reproduction. Each tier, signing the SAME payload with the SAME key (alice priv=1) via RFC 6979 deterministic ECDSA whose nonce HMAC uses PLAIN SHA-256, MUST produce the BYTE-IDENTICAL low-S DER signature listed in expected_sig. expected_payload = canonicalJson({...data, nonce, expiresAt}); expected_sig = low-S DER of deterministic ECDSA over sha256(expected_payload) signed directly (the digest is the message representative — do NOT re-hash). Generated via the TS reference (runar-ir-schema canonicalJsonStringify + @bsv/sdk primitives/ECDSA sign with forceLowS=true).

signing_vectors._notes: Non-ASCII BMP key (用户), astral-plane emoji key (🔥 = U+1F525), and a Latin-1 value (héllo). Exercises UTF-16 code-unit key ordering AND UTF-8 payload-byte hashing simultaneously: any tier that diverges on either canonicalization or nonce-hash will produce a different signature.

size_vectors_notes: F-296 (CL-GAP-088). The DoS size bound is hard-coded separately in every tier (TS InputLimits.MAX_IR_BYTES/MAX_STRING_BYTES, Go MaxEnvelope*Bytes, Rust/Python/Zig/Ruby/Java MAX_ENVELOPE_*_BYTES) and until now nothing pinned the seven values to each other or replayed a 'too-large' rejection. `size_limits` is the one shared source of truth: each tier asserts its own constants equal it. `size_vectors` is a GENERATION SPEC, not a literal -- a 16 MiB string does not belong in a checked-in fixture. To replay a vector, take `valid_envelope`, replace the named `field` (payload | sig | pubkey) with `length` ASCII 'x' characters (so bytes == chars in every tier), and call verifyEnvelope with verify_now_ms. expect_too_large=true: reason MUST be 'too-large' (the guard runs before JSON parse, hashing and ECDSA, so a tier that skips the guard returns a different reason or ok). expect_too_large=false (exactly at the limit): ok is false (the all-'x' field is not valid JSON / not a valid signature / not the signer's key) but reason MUST NOT be 'too-large' -- this catches an off-by-one guard (>= instead of >). Lengths are measured in UTF-8 bytes for payload and in characters for sig/pubkey, which coincide for ASCII.

size_vectors._notes: Exactly max_payload_bytes: passes the size guard, then fails on the later stage (bad-json).
Exactly max_field_bytes: passes the size guard.
Exactly max_field_bytes: passes the size guard.
